warmup.q: A thread holds the read lock of a ReentrantReadWriteLock. It then calls writeLock().lock() on the same lock. No other thread touches the lock. What happens?
options: It gets the write lock at once, because it is the only reader
It waits forever: the write lock waits for every reader to leave, and this thread is one of them
It gets the write lock and silently drops its read lock
warmup.why: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not support upgrading. The write lock needs zero readers, and the thread's own read lock counts. So the thread parks and never wakes. Nothing throws, and, as you'll see in this lesson, a thread dump does not even report it as a deadlock.

sections.h: ReentrantLock is synchronized with the controls exposed
sections.html:
ReentrantLock gives you the same guarantees as synchronized. Only one thread holds it at a time. Releasing it happens-before the next thread takes it, so the next owner sees every write the last owner made. And it is reentrant: the owner can take it again, and it counts the holds.

What you give up is the automatic release. A synchronized block always lets go when it exits, even on an exception. A ReentrantLock lets go only when you call unlock(). So every use follows one idiom:

Java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
private final List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>();   // guarded by lock

void post(Entry e) {
    lock.lock();               // before the try, never inside it
    try {
        entries.add(e);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();         // first line of finally: runs even if add throws
    }
}
Kotlin
private val lock = ReentrantLock()
private val entries = mutableListOf<Entry>()       // guarded by lock

fun post(e: Entry) {
    lock.withLock {            // kotlin.concurrent: lock(), try, finally unlock()
        entries += e
    }
}

lock() goes right before the try, not inside it. If it were inside and something failed before the lock was taken, the finally would release a lock you don't hold, and unlock() throws IllegalMonitorStateException. In Kotlin, withLock { } writes the whole pattern for you.

In return you get controls that synchronized doesn't have:

  • tryLock() takes the lock only if it is free right now, and returns false otherwise.
  • tryLock(200, MILLISECONDS) waits at most 200 ms. You met it in the previous lesson as a deadlock breaker.
  • lockInterruptibly() waits, but gives up with InterruptedException when the thread is interrupted. A thread waiting to enter synchronized ignores interrupts until it gets the monitor.
  • new ReentrantLock(true) makes a fair lock that hands over to the longest waiter.
  • isHeldByCurrentThread() and getQueueLength() let you assert and monitor.
  • Several Conditions per lock, which is the next section.

A thread waiting in lock() is parked, so a thread dump shows it as WAITING, not BLOCKED (lesson 2 of this track). Expect that when you read dumps of services that use explicit locks.

My rule: use synchronized for a short, simple critical section, and switch to ReentrantLock when you need one of these controls. The old reason to switch, pinning of virtual threads inside synchronized, mostly went away in JDK 24 (JEP 491). The virtual threads track covers that.

try.title: Three ways to wait for a busy lock
steps: Read TryLockDemo. A batch thread holds the ledger lock (and a monitor) for 1.5 seconds. api uses tryLock(200 ms), report uses lockInterruptibly(), and legacy waits on the monitor with synchronized.
Predict the order of the four output lines, and what getState() prints for report and legacy.
Run it. Then change api to wait 2 seconds instead of 200 ms and run it again.

code.title: TryLockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** A batch holds the ledger lock for 1.5 s. Three threads want in, each in a different way. */ public class TryLockDemo { static final ReentrantLock ledger = new ReentrantLock(); static final Object monitor = new Object(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread batch = new Thread(() -> { ledger.lock(); try { synchronized (monitor) { // the batch holds the lock AND a monitor pause(1_500); } } finally { ledger.unlock(); } }, "batch"); batch.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the batch get in first Thread api = new Thread(() -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { if (ledger.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // wait at most 200 ms try { System.out.println("api: got the lock"); } finally { ledger.unlock(); } } else { System.out.printf("api: gave up after %d ms and answered 503%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "api"); Thread report = new Thread(() -> { try { ledger.lockInterruptibly(); // an interrupt can cancel this wait try { System.out.println("report: got the lock"); } finally { ledger.unlock(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("report: interrupted while waiting, gave up cleanly"); } }, "report"); Thread legacy = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { // no way to give up here System.out.println("legacy: got the monitor at last, interrupted=" + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } }, "legacy"); api.start(); report.start(); legacy.start(); Thread.sleep(400); System.out.println("states: report=" + report.getState() + ", legacy=" + legacy.getState()); report.interrupt(); legacy.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {api, report, legacy, batch}) t.join(); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: TryLockDemo.kt

Three threads want in, each in a different way. private val ledger = ReentrantLock() private val monitor = Any() fun main() { val batch = thread(name = "batch") { ledger.withLock { synchronized(monitor) { // the batch holds the lock AND a monitor try { Thread.sleep(1_500) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } } Thread.sleep(100) // let the batch get in first val api = thread(start = false, name = "api") { val t0 = System.nanoTime() if (ledger.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // wait at most 200 ms try { println("api: got the lock") } finally { ledger.unlock() } } else { println("api: gave up after %d ms and answered 503".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } } val report = thread(start = false, name = "report") { try { ledger.lockInterruptibly() // an interrupt can cancel this wait try { println("report: got the lock") } finally { ledger.unlock() } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("report: interrupted while waiting, gave up cleanly") } } val legacy = thread(start = false, name = "legacy") { synchronized(monitor) { // no way to give up here println("legacy: got the monitor at last, interrupted=${Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted}") } } api.start() report.start() legacy.start() Thread.sleep(400) println("states: report=${report.state}, legacy=${legacy.state}") report.interrupt() legacy.interrupt() listOf(api, report, legacy, batch).forEach { it.join() } }

try.expect: api gives up after about 200 ms. The states are report=WAITING (parked on the lock) and legacy=BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor). The interrupt ends report's wait at once. legacy keeps waiting until the batch finishes, and only then sees interrupted=true. With a 2-second timeout, api gets the lock after the batch is done.

sections.h: Condition gives each reason to wait its own queue
sections.html:
A monitor has one wait set. In lesson 5 of this track that forced notifyAll() on the bounded buffer: producers and consumers waited in the same place, so a single notify() could wake the wrong kind of thread and stall everything.

A ReentrantLock can have as many wait sets as you like. Each call to lock.newCondition() makes one. await() plays the part of wait(): it releases the lock, parks, and takes the lock back before it returns. signal() and signalAll() play notify() and notifyAll(). Here is the producer side of the buffer:

Java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();    // producers wait here
private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();   // consumers wait here

public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await();   // releases the lock while waiting
        items.addLast(item);
        notEmpty.signal();                                   // wake one consumer
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val lock = ReentrantLock()
private val notFull = lock.newCondition()      // producers wait here
private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition()     // consumers wait here

fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock {
    while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await()   // releases the lock while waiting
    items.addLast(item)
    notEmpty.signal()                                 // wake one consumer
}

Only consumers ever wait on notEmpty, and one new item lets exactly one consumer proceed. Those are the two conditions under which lesson 5 said notify() is safe, and now they hold for each queue. So signal() is enough, and the other waiters stay asleep.

The rules from lesson 5 still apply:

  • You must hold the lock to call await() or signal(). Otherwise you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
  • Wait in a while loop. The Condition Javadoc allows spurious wake-ups, and another thread can take the item between the signal and your return from await().
  • Don't call wait() or notify() on a Condition. In Java it is an object like any other, so notFull.wait() compiles. It uses the condition object's own monitor, which you don't hold, and throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

Condition also has timed waits. awaitNanos(n) returns the time left, so a loop can keep waiting for the rest of a deadline. offer(item, timeout) in the lab uses it.

try.title: Count the wasted wake-ups
steps: Read WakeupCount. It moves 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer with 4 producers and 4 consumers. It does this twice: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with two Conditions and signal().
A wake-up is wasted when a thread wakes, re-checks its while condition, and has to wait again. Predict which version wastes more.
Run it twice and compare the counts and the times.

code.title: WakeupCount.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * 4 producers and 4 consumers move 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer, twice: * once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with notFull/notEmpty and signal(). * A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, and has to wait again. */ public class WakeupCount { static final class Buffer { final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); final Condition notFull; final Condition notEmpty; final boolean shared; final ArrayDeque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); long wasted; // guarded by lock Buffer(boolean oneCondition) { shared = oneCondition; notFull = lock.newCondition(); notEmpty = oneCondition ? notFull : lock.newCondition(); // same queue, or two } void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == 1) { notFull.await(); if (items.size() == 1) wasted++; // woke up for nothing } items.add(x); if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll(); else notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } int take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await(); if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++; } int x = items.remove(); if (shared) notFull.signalAll(); else notFull.signal(); return x; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (boolean one : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Buffer buffer = new Buffer(one); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.put(n); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : threads) t.start(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)%n", one ? "one condition, signalAll():" : "notFull + notEmpty, signal():", buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } }

alt.title: WakeupCount.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // 4 producers and 4 consumers move 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer, twice: // once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with notFull/notEmpty and signal(). // A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, and has to wait again. private class CountingBuffer(private val shared: Boolean) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull: Condition = lock.newCondition() private val notEmpty: Condition = if (shared) notFull else lock.newCondition() // same queue, or two private val items = ArrayDeque<Int>() var wasted = 0L // guarded by lock private set fun put(x: Int) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == 1) { notFull.await() if (items.size == 1) wasted++ // woke up for nothing } items.addLast(x) if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll() else notEmpty.signal() } fun take(): Int = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await() if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++ } val x = items.removeFirst() if (shared) notFull.signalAll() else notFull.signal() x } } fun main() { for (one in listOf(true, false)) { val buffer = CountingBuffer(one) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = (1..4).flatMap { listOf( thread { repeat(5_000) { n -> buffer.put(n) } }, thread { repeat(5_000) { buffer.take() } }, ) } threads.forEach { it.join() } val label = if (one) "one condition, signalAll():" else "notFull + notEmpty, signal():" println("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)".format(label, buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } }

try.expect: With one condition, tens of thousands of wake-ups are wasted (80,000 to 90,000 in runs here), because every signalAll() wakes all seven other threads and most of them go back to sleep. With two conditions, the count drops to hundreds or a few thousand, and the run is several times faster. It isn't zero, because of barging: a running thread can grab the lock and the item before the signalled thread wakes up. That is why the while loop stays.

sections.h: ReadWriteLock lets readers share, and never lets them upgrade
sections.html:
An FX rate cache is read 5,000 times a second and refreshed every 5 seconds. With a plain lock, every reader waits for every other reader, although readers never conflict. A ReentrantReadWriteLock has two locks inside: many threads can hold the read lock together, and the write lock is exclusive. It waits until no reader and no writer is inside.

Java
private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new HashMap<>();   // guarded by rw

BigDecimal rate(String pair) {
    rw.readLock().lock();                 // many threads can hold this at once
    try {
        return rates.get(pair);
    } finally {
        rw.readLock().unlock();
    }
}

void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) {
    rw.writeLock().lock();                // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock
    try {
        rates.clear();
        rates.putAll(fresh);
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock()
private val rates = HashMap<String, BigDecimal>()    // guarded by rw

fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rw.read {     // many threads can hold this at once
    rates[pair]
}

fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) = rw.write {   // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock
    rates.clear()
    rates.putAll(fresh)
}

The trap is the cache miss. The natural code checks under the read lock and, if the rate is missing, takes the write lock to load it:

Java
rw.readLock().lock();
try {
    BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair);
    if (r != null) return r;
    rw.writeLock().lock();         // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever
    try {
        r = loader.apply(pair);
        rates.put(pair, r);
        return r;
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock();
    }
} finally {
    rw.readLock().unlock();
}
Kotlin
rw.readLock().lock()
try {
    val r = rates[pair]
    if (r != null) return r
    rw.writeLock().lock()         // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever
    try {
        return loader(pair).also { rates[pair] = it }
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock()
    }
} finally {
    rw.readLock().unlock()
}

That is a lock upgrade, and ReentrantReadWriteLock doesn't support it. The write lock waits for all readers to leave. This thread is a reader, and it won't leave until it gets the write lock. It waits forever, on its own. Two threads doing it at once wait for each other.

Worse, the JVM's deadlock detector says nothing. Run the demo with -Pargs=hang and take a thread dump: main is WAITING (parking) in WriteLock.lock, there is no Found one Java-level deadlock, and Thread.print -l lists Locked ownable synchronizers: None. Read locks have no single owner, so the detector has no cycle to find.

The fix: release the read lock, take the write lock, and check again, because another thread may have loaded the rate while you held nothing. Going the other way, a downgrade, is allowed: while holding the write lock, take the read lock, then release the write lock.

A read-write lock pays off when reads are frequent, take a while, and writes are rare. For a map lookup that takes 50 ns, the extra bookkeeping can cost more than it saves. When the cache is replaced as a whole, a volatile reference to an immutable map is simpler and faster still. Lesson 11 of this track shows that pattern.

try.title: Upgrade, then downgrade
steps: Run UpgradeDeadlock. It tries the upgrade with tryLock(1, SECONDS) so it can't hang, then does a downgrade.
Run the Kotlin twin. Its last line puts write { } inside read { }. Predict: does it hang?
Optional: run the Java one with -Pargs=hang. In a second terminal run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l with the printed PID and look at main. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

code.title: UpgradeDeadlock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. * Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. * Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. */ public class UpgradeDeadlock { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); boolean hang = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("hang"); // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock(); try { System.out.println("holding the read lock, read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); if (hang) { System.out.println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", Ctrl+C to stop)"); rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, us included } boolean got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // the same wait, with a time limit System.out.println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: " + got); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock(); try { rw.readLock().lock(); // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } try { System.out.println("downgraded: write locked = " + rw.isWriteLocked() + ", read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } }

Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. // Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. // Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() val hang = args.firstOrNull() == "hang" // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock() try { println("holding the read lock, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") if (hang) { println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()}, Ctrl+C to stop)") rw.writeLock().lock() // waits for every reader to leave, us included } val got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // the same wait, with a time limit println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: $got") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock() try { rw.readLock().lock() // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock() } try { println("downgraded: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 3. Kotlin only: write {} inside read {} does not hang, because write {} first lets go of // this thread's read locks. That makes it a release-then-acquire, not an atomic upgrade. rw.read { rw.write { println("kotlin write {} inside read {}: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } } }

try.expect: write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: false, then downgraded: write locked = false, read holds = 1. The Kotlin write { } inside read { } does not hang: it prints write locked = true, read holds = 0, because Kotlin's write lets go of this thread's read locks first. With -Pargs=hang, the dump shows main parked in WriteLock.lock and no deadlock report.

sections.h: StampedLock trades safety rails for speed
sections.html:
Even a read lock writes to shared memory: every reader increments and decrements the lock's count. On a hot path with many cores, that one cache line bounces between them. StampedLock (JDK 8) adds a mode with no write at all, the optimistic read:

Java
long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();   // 1. no lock, just a version number
long b = bid, a = ask;                   // 2. copy into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock();             // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = bid; a = ask; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); }
}
return new Quote(b, a);                  // 5. use the locals only after validate
Kotlin
var stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead()     // 1. no lock, just a version number
var b = bid; var a = ask                 // 2. copy into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock()              // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = bid; a = ask } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp) }
}
return Quote(b, a)                       // 5. use the locals only after validate

tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp, a version number of the lock (or 0 if a writer holds it). You read the fields into locals with no lock held. Then validate(stamp) asks: did any writer get in since that stamp? If not, your copies are consistent. If yes, you throw them away and read again under a real read lock.

Between steps 2 and 3, the copies can be garbage: a new bid with an old ask. The Javadoc only promises that writes happen-before your reads if a later validate returns true. So the code between the stamp and the validation must not act on the values. No loops driven by them, no array index, no calls that could throw. Copy, validate, then use.

The price of the speed is a list of things StampedLock doesn't do:

  • It is not reentrant. A thread that holds the write lock and asks for it again waits for itself.
  • It has no Conditions.
  • Stamps are not tied to a thread, and you must pass the right stamp to unlockRead or unlockWrite.

Use it for a small group of fields that are read on a hot path and written rarely, such as a quote's bid and ask, and only after a profiler shows the read-write lock is the cost. For most code ReentrantReadWriteLock, or no lock at all, is the better choice.

try.title: Catch torn reads with validate()
steps: Read OptimisticRead. A writer keeps updating a quote, and ask is always bid + 2 once a write is done. The reader counts how many optimistic reads saw a quote where that isn't true.
Predict: will any torn quote get past validate()?
Run it. Then delete the validate check (treat every optimistic read as good) and count the torn quotes yourself.

code.title: OptimisticRead.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock; /** * A writer keeps moving an FX quote; the ask is always bid + 2. A reader reads both fields * optimistically for one second and counts how often validate() caught a half-written quote. */ public class OptimisticRead { static final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock(); static long bid = 100, ask = 102; // guarded by lock; ask == bid + 2 when no write is in progress static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { long v = 100; while (!done) { long stamp = lock.writeLock(); try { bid = ++v; for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // widens the half-written moment ask = v + 2; } finally { lock.unlockWrite(stamp); } } }); writer.start(); long reads = 0, failed = 0, tornCaught = 0, tornPassed = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock taken, just a version number long b = bid, a = ask; // 2. copy the fields into locals boolean torn = a - b != 2; if (lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++; // never happens } else { failed++; if (torn) tornCaught++; stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = bid; a = ask; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } } done = true; writer.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn quotes caught: %,d torn quotes that passed validate(): %d%n", reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed); } }

alt.title: OptimisticRead.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A writer keeps moving an FX quote; the ask is always bid + 2. A reader reads both fields // optimistically for one second and counts how often validate() caught a half-written quote. private class Quote { val lock = StampedLock() var bid = 100L // guarded by lock; ask == bid + 2 when no write is in progress var ask = 102L } @Volatile private var done = false fun main() { val q = Quote() val writer = thread { var v = 100L while (!done) { val stamp = q.lock.writeLock() try { q.bid = ++v repeat(20) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // widens the half-written moment q.ask = v + 2 } finally { q.lock.unlockWrite(stamp) } } } var reads = 0L; var failed = 0L; var tornCaught = 0L; var tornPassed = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ var stamp = q.lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock taken, just a version number var b = q.bid; var a = q.ask // 2. copy the fields into locals val torn = a - b != 2L if (q.lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++ // never happens } else { failed++ if (torn) tornCaught++ stamp = q.lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = q.bid; a = q.ask } finally { q.lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } } done = true writer.join() println("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn quotes caught: %,d torn quotes that passed validate(): %d" .format(reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed)) }

try.expect: Thousands of reads fail validation each second, and many of those saw a torn quote (a new bid with an old ask). The last number, torn quotes that passed validate(), is always 0. Without the check, those torn quotes would have gone to the caller.

analogy: A ReentrantLock is a meeting room with a screen outside. You can queue for the room (lock), glance at the screen and leave if it's busy (tryLock), queue for at most two minutes (tryLock(timeout)), or leave the queue when your phone rings (lockInterruptibly). Conditions are separate waiting areas: people waiting for a projector don't get woken when a chair frees up. A read-write lock is a museum gallery: many visitors at once, but the cleaner needs it empty. A visitor can't become the cleaner without walking out first, and if they wait inside for the room to empty, they wait forever. The analogy breaks in one place: a person in the room always leaves eventually. A thread that forgets unlock() holds the room for the life of the process.
world: A Quarkus payment service usually has two lock shapes. One is a per-key lock around a check-and-update, such as a card's daily spend, where tryLock(50 ms) lets a request fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up a worker thread behind a stuck holder. The other is a read-mostly cache, such as FX rates or BIN ranges, refreshed by a scheduled job and read by every request. For the cache, a read-write lock works, but check whether the refresh replaces the whole map. If it does, a volatile reference to an immutable map needs no lock at all. In Kotlin services, prefer withLock, read and write, and remember that write inside read releases the read lock first, so re-check whatever made you decide to write.
mistake: The most common mistake is a lock() without a finally, or with code between lock() and try that can throw. One exception on a rare path, a validation error or a timeout from a downstream call, skips the unlock(). The lock is now held by a thread that has moved on. Every other thread parks in ReentrantLock.lock(), and a dump shows dozens of threads WAITING (parking) while Thread.print -l names an owner that is idle somewhere else. Nothing ever releases it. The fix is the idiom, every time: lock() on the line before try, unlock() as the first line of finally. In Kotlin, use withLock { } and the problem can't happen.

compare.title: A read-mostly cache in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; // 1. fast path under the read lock } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); // 2. let go BEFORE asking for the write lock } rw.writeLock().lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, loader); // 3. re-check under the write lock } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rw.read { rates[pair] ?: rw.write { // write {} let go of our read lock first, so another thread may have loaded it: re-check rates.getOrPut(pair) { loader(pair) } } }

compare.note: The Java version must release the read lock before taking the write lock, or it hangs. The Kotlin version looks like an upgrade, and it doesn't hang, because the standard library's ReentrantReadWriteLock.write releases every read lock this thread holds, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Its documentation warns that this upgrade is not atomic: another thread can write in the gap, so anything you checked before write must be checked again inside it. That is why both versions re-check (computeIfAbsent, getOrPut). Kotlin's helpers remove the ceremony, not the reasoning.

worked.title: A per-card lock that fails fast

steps.say: Authorizations for one card must run one at a time, because each one checks and then updates that card's daily spend. Different cards must not wait for each other. And if one holder gets stuck, other requests for that card should fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up worker threads. Read the solution and its subgoal labels.
steps.code: class CardLocks { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); <T> T withCard(String cardId, Duration maxWait, Supplier<T> action) throws InterruptedException { // 1. one lock per card, created at most once ReentrantLock lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(cardId, id -> new ReentrantLock()); // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new CardBusyException(cardId); // 3. busy: fail fast, the client retries } try { return action.get(); // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); // 5. always release } } }

alt.html: class CardLocks { private val locks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock>() fun <T> withCard(cardId: String, maxWait: Duration, action: () -> T): T { // 1. one lock per card, created at most once val lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(cardId) { ReentrantLock() } // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw CardBusyException(cardId) // 3. busy: fail fast, the client retries } try { return action() // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock() // 5. always release } } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself: why does tryLock sit outside the try, when unlock() is inside the finally? Answer: if tryLock returns false or throws InterruptedException, this thread doesn't hold the lock. A finally that called unlock() would throw IllegalMonitorStateException and hide the real result. Only the code that runs while you hold the lock goes inside the try.

Why not synchronized (cardId)? Two Strings with the same contents are often different objects, so two requests for the same card could each lock their own string and run together. Interned strings go the other way: unrelated code that locks the same literal shares your lock (lesson 4 of this track). And synchronized has no timeout. A map of real lock objects avoids all three problems.

One problem remains: the map gains a lock for every card it ever sees, and never shrinks. With millions of cards that is memory you don't get back. Removing entries safely is harder than it looks, because a thread may be about to lock the entry you remove. The usual answer is lock striping: a fixed array of locks, chosen by hash.
steps.code: private final ReentrantLock[] stripes = new ReentrantLock[256]; { for (int i = 0; i < stripes.length; i++) stripes[i] = new ReentrantLock(); } ReentrantLock lockFor(String cardId) { return stripes[Math.floorMod(cardId.hashCode(), stripes.length)]; // two cards may share a stripe: fine }

alt.html: private val stripes = Array(256) { ReentrantLock() } fun lockFor(cardId: String): ReentrantLock = stripes[Math.floorMod(cardId.hashCode(), stripes.size)] // two cards may share a stripe: fine

steps.say: Two cards that share a stripe now wait for each other. That costs a little throughput and nothing in correctness. If you ever hold two card locks at once, for a transfer between cards, take the stripes in index order, as in lesson 6 of this track, and skip the second lock when both cards land on the same stripe.

lab.title: A buffer with two conditions and a cache that doesn't hang
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The five LockBuffer tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. Two FxRateCache tests time out (the upgrade hang), and the snapshot test reports mixed refreshes.
Part 1: write LockBuffer with one ReentrantLock and two Conditions, notFull and notEmpty. Check the capacity in the constructor. put and take follow the shape in the second section, with signal().
Write offer(item, timeout): the same as put, but wait with notFull.awaitNanos(remaining) and return false when the time runs out.
Part 2: fix FxRateCache.rate. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check before calling the loader, so the loader runs once per pair.
Fix snapshot so it reads every pair under one read lock. Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: awaitNanos returns the nanoseconds still left (zero or less when time is up). Keep the returned value and pass it to the next awaitNanos in the loop.
Use lock.lockInterruptibly() at the top of put, take and offer, so an interrupted thread doesn't wait for the lock either. await() already throws InterruptedException when interrupted.
The cache's HashMap is fine as it is: every access to it happens under the read or the write lock. Only the order in which you take the locks is wrong.
lab.done: All eight tests in ExplicitLocksTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Two conditions from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a bounded buffer with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions: put waits while full, take waits while empty. Check: is every unlock() in a finally, every await() in a while, and does each method signal the other side's condition?

answer.html: class Buffer<T> { private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition(); private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; Buffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await(); items.addLast(item); notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } T take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await(); T head = items.removeFirst(); notFull.signal(); return head; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class Buffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull = lock.newCondition() private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await() items.addLast(item) notEmpty.signal() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await() items.removeFirst().also { notFull.signal() } } }

recap: ReentrantLock gives the same exclusion and visibility as synchronized, but you release it yourself: lock() before try, unlock() first in finally, or Kotlin's withLock.
Reach for it when you need tryLock, a timeout, lockInterruptibly, fairness, or more than one condition.
Each Condition is its own wait queue. With one queue per kind of waiter, signal() is enough. Still wait in a while loop.
A read-write lock lets readers share. Upgrading from read to write hangs forever, and the deadlock detector won't report it. Release, take the write lock, re-check.
StampedLock optimistic reads take no lock at all. Copy into locals, validate, and only then use the values. It is not reentrant.
Threads waiting on explicit locks show as WAITING (parking) in a dump, not BLOCKED.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Should we replace all our synchronized blocks with ReentrantLock? I heard it's faster." Explain what you would tell them.
explain.answer: Not by default. Both give the same mutual exclusion and visibility, and on current JDKs their speed is similar for ordinary critical sections. synchronized can't leak: it releases on every exit. With ReentrantLock you must release in a finally, and one missed path holds the lock forever. I'd switch only where we need something synchronized can't do: give up after a timeout with tryLock, let an interrupt cancel the wait with lockInterruptibly, use a fair lock, or have separate conditions for different kinds of waiters. For read-mostly data I'd look at a read-write lock, or better, an immutable snapshot behind a volatile reference.

deeper.html:
ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, Semaphore and CountDownLatch are all built on one class, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS). It keeps one int of state and a queue of waiting threads. For ReentrantLock the state is the hold count; for a semaphore it is the number of permits left; for a latch it is the count. A thread that can't proceed joins the queue and parks with LockSupport.park. That is why it shows as WAITING in a dump, with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync). A release unparks the next thread in the queue.

In non-fair mode, the default, a thread that arrives just as the lock is released can take it before the queued thread wakes. That is barging, and it is why the two-condition buffer in the second Try it still wasted some wake-ups. It is also why non-fair locks have much higher throughput: waking a parked thread takes microseconds, and a running thread can take and release the lock many times in that gap. Fair mode closes the gap and pays the wake-up cost on every hand-off. Even on a fair lock, the untimed tryLock() barges: its Javadoc says it does not honor the fairness setting.

ReentrantReadWriteLock splits its 32-bit state into two 16-bit halves, one for read holds and one for write holds. That is why its Javadoc caps it at 65,535 recursive write locks and 65,535 read locks.

StampedLock also has tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp), which upgrades a read or optimistic stamp to a write stamp if no other thread is in the way, and returns 0 if it can't. It is the only upgrade in the JDK's locks, and it can fail, so you still need the fallback path.

If you ever build your own synchronizer, subclass AQS and implement tryAcquire and tryRelease; its Javadoc has a small Mutex example. First check java.util.concurrent for one that already exists. Lesson 10 of this track covers the common ones.
